question.text:
The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $\mathbf r(t) = 3\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as

\[ \mathbf n = \dfrac{a(t)\,\mathbf i + b(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||}. \] Find the function $a(t).$
question.explanation:
For convenience, we express $\mathbf r(t)$ in column vector notation:

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3\cos t \\ 4\sin t\end{bmatrix} \]

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

Step 1: We compute the tangent vector $\mathbf r'(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \begin{bmatrix} x'(t) \\ y'(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3\sin t \\ 4\cos t\end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Rotating the vector $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise, we get

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -3\sin t \\ 4\cos t\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4\cos t \\ 3\sin t\end{bmatrix}. \]

Step 3: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of $\mathbf r'(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf n &= \dfrac{1}{||\mathbf r'(t)||}\begin{bmatrix} 4\cos t \\ 3\sin t\end{bmatrix} =\dfrac{4\cos t\,\mathbf i + 3\sin t\,\mathbf j }{||\mathbf r'(t)||}. \end{align*}

Finally, we conclude that $a(t) = 4\cos t.$

question.text: The closed curve $C$ is defined as $x^2+y^2 = 9.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
question.explanation:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3\cos t \\ 3\sin t\end{bmatrix},\qquad t \in [0,2\pi) \]

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

Step 1: We compute the tangent vector $\mathbf r'(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \begin{bmatrix} x'(t) \\ y'(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3\sin t \\ 3\cos t\end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Rotating the vector $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise, we get

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -3\sin t \\ 3\cos t\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3\cos t \\ 3\sin t\end{bmatrix}. \]

Step 3: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of $\mathbf r'(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since

\[ ||\mathbf r'(t)|| = \sqrt{(-3\sin t)^2 + (3\cos t)^2} = 3, \]

and since for our curve $x(t) = 3\cos{t}$ and $y(t) = 3\sin{t},$ it follows that

\begin{align*} \mathbf n &= \dfrac{1}{||\mathbf r'(t)||}\begin{bmatrix} 3\cos t \\ 3\sin t\end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 3\cos t \\ 3\sin t\end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y\end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
The closed curve $C$ is defined as $\mathbf r(t) = 6\sin t\,\mathbf{i} + 6\cos t \,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector for $C$ can be expressed as

\[ \mathbf n = \dfrac{a(t)\,\mathbf i + b(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||}. \] Find the function $b(t).$

Hint: Observe that $C$ is traversed clockwise.
question.explanation:
For convenience, we express $\mathbf r(t)$ in column vector notation:

\[ \mathbf r(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6\sin t \\ 6\cos t \end{bmatrix} \]

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, negatively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

Step 1: We compute the tangent vector $\mathbf r'(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \begin{bmatrix} x'(t) \\ y'(t)\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6\cos t \\ -6\sin t \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Step 2: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ counterclockwise to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a $90^\circ$ counterclockwise rotation is

\[ R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Rotating the vector $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ counterclockwise, we get

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 6\cos t \\ -6\sin t\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6\sin t \\ 6\cos t \end{bmatrix}. \]

Step 3: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of $\mathbf r'(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf n &= \dfrac{1}{||\mathbf r'(t)||} \begin{bmatrix} 6\sin t \\ 6\cos t \end{bmatrix} =\dfrac{6\sin t\,\mathbf i + 6\cos t \,\mathbf j }{||\mathbf r'(t)||}. \end{align*}

Finally, we conclude that $b(t) = 6\cos t .$
